title: Where the giant group appears
hook: Double the random friendships. Does the biggest group of friends double too?

knows: people can be linked in pairs
connected means a chain of links
doesNotKnow: random links make one huge group appear suddenly, not gradually

misconception: Doubling the number of random links roughly doubles the size of the biggest connected group.
objective: The learner can explain that connection does not grow in proportion to links: past about one friend each, small groups join into one giant group that holds most people (200 people: 18% at 100 links, 74% at 200).

claims.text: In the lesson's world of 200 people (seed 1), 100 random friendships give a biggest connected group of 36 people (18%) and 200 friendships give 148 people (74%); 50 give 9, 150 give 110 (55%) and 300 give 183 (92%).
claims.source: model.ts: mulberry32(1); each link is a random pair a != b not already linked (a = floor(rng()*200), b = floor(rng()*200)); the first m links form the world with m links; biggest group by union-find. Node re-run reproduces 9, 36, 110, 148, 183 at m = 50, 100, 150, 200, 300 (183/200 = 91.5%, shown rounded as 92%; 9/200 = 4.5% shown as 5%). Seed 1 was the first seed tried, but it is one world: see c2 for the spread.

claims.text: Across 20 random worlds of 200 people the biggest group averages 16.8% at one friend each and 79.4% at two (not shown to learners as a number; the lesson shows one world).
claims.source: Same rule as c1 with seeds 1 to 20; means 3.9%, 16.8%, 59.1%, 79.4%, 94.0% at 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3 friends each; at 2.0 the 20 seeds range 72.0% to 85.5%. Re-run in node by the builder.

claims.text: In random links among a very large crowd, a giant group appears once the average number of friends passes one; at two friends each it holds about 80% of people.
claims.source: Erdős and Rényi (1960), On the evolution of random graphs, Publ. Math. Inst. Hung. Acad. Sci. 5: 17-61. Large-n share S solves S = 1 - exp(-cS): 79.7% at c = 2, 58.3% at c = 1.5, 94.1% at c = 3. The threshold at average degree 1 is Erdős-Rényi, not derived in the book ch. 2. Fact-checker to confirm the citation. Reveal states only the threshold ('near one friend each').

claims.text: With 200 people, 100 links is one friend each on average, and the average number of friends is 2 x links / people (50 links 0.5, 100 links 1.0, 150 links 1.5, 200 links 2.0, 300 links 3.0).
claims.source: Each link gives one friend to each of its two people, so total friends = 2 x links; average = 2 x links / 200.

claims.text: Early on a new random link usually joins two small groups; once groups are big, a new link between two of them merges both, so one giant group absorbs most of the crowd.
claims.source: Mechanism of the union-find run in model.ts: the biggest group grows by the size of whatever it merges with. Qualitative; consistent with c1 and c3. Fact-checker to confirm wording is not overclaiming ('usually').

claims.text: The lesson is a model of random links in one made-up crowd; real networks are not claimed to behave this way.
claims.source: Scope statement. Easley and Kleinberg (2010), Networks, Crowds, and Markets, ch. 2 §2.2 (section unconfirmed), defines the giant component and shows it in real networks. No real-data numbers are stated in the lesson. Fact-checker to confirm the section.

recall.question: A crowd of 1,000 people makes random friendships, starting from none. Roughly when does one big connected group appear?
options: Gradually, in proportion to the friendships
Suddenly, once people have about one friend each on average
Only when everyone has at least 10 friends
recall.why: Past about one friend each, small groups join into one giant group that holds most people; below it, groups stay small.
